'''''Sporobolus pumilus''''', the '''saltmeadow cordgrass''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SPPA|taxon=Spartina patens|accessdate=24 November 2015}}</ref> also known as '''salt hay''', is a species of [[cordgrass]] native to the Atlantic coast of the [[Americas]], from [[Newfoundland and Labrador|Newfoundland]] south along the eastern United States to the [[Caribbean]] and north-eastern Mexico. It was reclassified after a taxonomic revision in 2014,<ref>Peterson, PM, et al (2014) A molecular phylogeny and new subgeneric classification of Sporobolus (Poaceae: Chloridoideae: Sporobolinae), Taxon 63: 1212-1243.</ref> but the older name, '''''Spartina patens''''', may still be found in use. It can be found in marshlands in other areas of the world as an [[introduced species]] and often a harmful [[noxious weed]] or [[invasive species]].

It is a perennial [[grass]] found in the upper areas of brackish [[coast]]al [[salt marsh]]es. It is a slender and wiry plant that grows in thick mats {{convert|12|to|24|in|cm|-1}} high, green in spring and summer, and turns light brown in late fall and winter. The stems are wispy and hollow, and the [[Leaf|leaves]] roll inward and appear round. Because its stems are weak, the wind and water action can bend the grass, creating the appearance of a field of tufts and [[cowlick]]s. Like its relative [[smooth cordgrass]], saltmeadow cordgrass produces [[flower]]s and [[seed]]s on only one side of the stalk. Flowers are a deep purple from June to October and turn brown in the winter months.

Saltmeadow cordgrass is found in [[high marsh]] zones where it is covered at times by high [[tide]]s. Specialized cells are able to exclude salt from entering the roots, preventing the loss of fresh water. This grass is, however, less tolerant of saltwater than some other marsh grasses. It can also grow on beaches and can quickly recolonize an [[overwash]] zone.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lonard|first1=Robert I.|last2=Judd|first2=Frank W.|last3=Stalter|first3=Richard|date=2010-09-01|title=The Biological Flora of Coastal Dunes and Wetlands: Spartina patens (W. Aiton) G.H. Muhlenberg|journal=Journal of Coastal Research|volume=265|pages=935–946|doi=10.2112/JCOASTRES-D-09-00154.1|s2cid=129228658|issn=0749-0208}}</ref>

A healthy salt marsh depends on the presence of plants such as salt hay grass and smooth cordgrass. These grasses provide rich habitat for [[crustacean]]s, [[Mollusca|mollusks]], and birds, and serve as a major source of [[organic matter|organic]] [[nutrient]]s for the entire [[estuary]]. Mats of salt hay grass are inhabited by many small animals and are an important food source for ducks and [[Ammodramus|seaside sparrows]].
[[Image:Martin Johnson Heade - Newburyport Meadows ATC.jpg|thumb|left|''[[Newburyport, Massachusetts|Newburyport]] [[salt marsh|Meadows]]'', c. 1872–1878, by [[Martin Johnson Heade]]]]
[[File:Spartina patens-saltmeadow cordgrass.jpg|thumb|left|''Sporobolus pumilus'' in a [[high marsh]] area]]

Saltmeadow cordgrass marshes serve as pollution filters and as buffers against flooding and shoreline erosion. During the [[Colonial America|colonial era]], towns scattered from [[Narragansett Bay]] to the [[Gulf of Maine]] were often settled based on their proximity to salt marshes due to the importance of saltmeadow cordgrass for [[fodder]]. It was harvested for bedding and fodder for farm animals and for garden [[mulch]]. Before [[hay]] was baled and stored under cover, it was used to top the hay stacks in the fields.

Many of the salt marshes in [[Rhode Island]] have been severely affected by filling, development, and road construction. These alterations restrict [[tidal flow]], often having a severe [[ecology|ecological]] impact on the marsh. Because saltmeadow cordgrass requires a salty, wet habitat, restricted tidal flow often dries out the marsh and encourages the growth of invasive freshwater plants. Saltmeadow and smooth cordgrasses are often out-competed for space by [[Phragmites|common reed]] in areas where human activity has disturbed or altered the marsh. Common reed is not as productive or beneficial to a salt marsh as cordgrass.

While this species is a key member of the salt marsh flora in its native habitat, it is known as a harmful [[invasive species]] in other parts of the world. It is a notorious pest in the [[San Francisco Bay Area]], where it out-competes native plants such as [[soft bird's beak]] and alters the habitat of rare animals such as [[Ridgway's rail]].<ref>[http://spartina.org/species/spartina-patens_v2.pdf Spartina.org Fact Sheet]</ref> This cordgrass was introduced to the [[estuary|estuaries]] of [[Oregon]] with shipments of [[oyster]]s and has been dominating and crowding out native vegetation there.<ref>[http://www.oregon.gov/ODA/PLANT/WEEDS/profile_saltmeadowcordgrass.shtml Oregon Noxious Weeds]</ref> It has appeared in marshes on the [[Iberian Peninsula]], where it threatens native plant [[biodiversity]].<ref>{{cite book |author=D.
